title: List, Dictionary, HashSet, and Queue (generic collections)
hook: Most day-to-day C# code stores data in four generic types from System.Collections.Generic. Each one answers a different question: append, look up, check membership, or process in order.

blocks.text: The Base Class Library (BCL) ships ready-made collection types in System.Collections.Generic. List<T> is a growable buffer — think of it as an array that resizes itself. Dictionary<TKey, TValue> maps keys to values for fast lookup, like a Redis cache keyed by session ID. HashSet<T> stores unique items and answers "is this already in the set?" in near-constant time. Queue<T> is first-in-first-out (FIFO): enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front.

entries.plainDefinition: The standard set of types shipped with .NET — collections, I/O, networking, and more.
entries.example: List<int> and Dictionary<string, string> are BCL types.

entries.plainDefinition: A growable array with an Add method and O(1) indexing by position.
A hash table that maps unique keys to values with O(1) average lookup.
A set of unique items with fast Contains checks — a dictionary without values.
A first-in-first-out (FIFO) collection: Enqueue adds to the back, Dequeue removes from the front.

blocks.text: Choosing the wrong collection is how you end up scanning 50,000 keys on every HTTP request. An SQS batch is a List. A Redis-shaped cache is a Dictionary. Checking whether you already processed a message ID is a HashSet, not List.Contains in a loop. None of these types are thread-safe by default — two threads calling Add on the same List without a lock corrupts the backing array.

blocks.title: Match the type to the question
blocks.body: Append? List. Lookup by key? Dictionary. Uniqueness? HashSet. Process in arrival order? Queue. In-process Dictionary is not Redis; in-process Queue is not SQS.

items.title: List<T> — growable buffer
items.body: Add is amortized O(1). Indexer is O(1). Insert at position 0 is O(n) because every item shifts. Set Capacity in the constructor when you know the size upfront.

items.title: Dictionary<TKey, TValue> — key lookup
items.body: Requires hash and equality on TKey via IEqualityComparer<TKey>. TryGetValue is the safe lookup pattern. When Count exceeds the load factor (~72% of bucket count), Dictionary doubles its bucket array and rehashes every entry — a gen-0 GC spike if you grow a huge map in one loop. Duplicate keys throw on Add; the indexer overwrites silently.

items.title: HashSet<T> — uniqueness
items.body: Add returns false if the item was already present. Contains is O(1) average — far faster than List.Contains for large collections.

items.title: Queue<T> and Stack<T> — ordered access
items.body: Queue is FIFO (Enqueue/Dequeue). Stack is last-in-first-out (LIFO) with Push/Pop. LinkedList<T> is almost never the interview answer.

diagram.title: Collection decision tree
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  Q{What do you need?}
  Q -->|Append items| L[List T]
  Q -->|Look up by key| D[Dictionary TKey TValue]
  Q -->|Check membership| H[HashSet T]
  Q -->|Process in order| F{Order?}
  F -->|First in first out| QU[Queue T]
  F -->|Last in first out| ST[Stack T]

snippet.label: SQS batch with cache lookup
snippet.explanation: List holds the batch. Dictionary is the cache-shaped lookup keyed by message ID. Four types, four questions — each does one job well.

snippet.label: HashSet and Queue for dedup and retry
snippet.explanation: HashSet answers "have we seen this ID?" in O(1). Queue holds failed messages in FIFO order for retry processing.

snippet.label: Dictionary comparer for string keys
snippet.explanation: string keys should pick a comparer: Ordinal for IDs, OrdinalIgnoreCase for HTTP headers. Without a comparer, case-sensitive matching surprises you in production.

snippet.label: Dictionary resize and capacity hint
snippet.explanation: Dictionary grows by doubling bucket count when load factor is exceeded. Pre-sizing with the expected count avoids repeated resize-and-rehash cycles that show up as GC pressure in production.

snippet.label: Custom IEqualityComparer for struct keys
snippet.explanation: Struct keys do not get automatic equality. If GetHashCode and Equals disagree — or you change the hash after insert — lookups silently fail. Always pass the same comparer to Dictionary and HashSet.

blocks.title: C# collections versus JS Map and Set
rows: C# List is generic with known T; JS Array is dynamically typed and grows with push()
Map uses SameValueZero equality; Dictionary uses IEqualityComparer — struct keys need a custom comparer
Both O(1) average Contains; JS Set uses reference or primitive equality, not configurable
JS object keys coerce to strings; Dictionary<K,V> keeps Guid, int, or struct keys natively
C# Queue is a dedicated FIFO type; JS shift() is O(n) on Array
C# has thread-safe maps in System.Collections.Concurrent; Node shares one thread

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using List.Contains in a hot loop instead of HashSet — O(n) per check versus O(1). Forgetting a StringComparer and treating JWT issuer URLs as case-sensitive when they were mixed case. Sharing a List across SQS handler tasks without synchronization — two threads calling Add corrupts the backing array.

blocks.text: Dictionary<TKey,TValue> stores entries in a bucket array; each bucket is a singly-linked chain of Entry structs. Lookup computes bucketIndex = hashCode & (bucketCount - 1) using the IEqualityComparer, then walks the chain calling Equals. List<T> holds a T[] _items array and int _size; when _size == _items.Length, it allocates a new array at roughly double capacity and copies. HashSet<T> is literally a Dictionary<T,T> with dummy values. How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters monitor System.Runtime --counters gen-0-gc-count,gc-heap-size while bulk-loading a Dictionary without a capacity hint — you will see gen-0 spikes on each resize.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Pure speed when order does not matter

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "Dictionary is always O(1)" without mentioning hash collisions, comparer choice, or resize cost. Saying "I'd scan the List to find duplicates" on a 100k-item collection — that is O(n²). Strong answer: HashSet for membership, pre-size Dictionary with expected count, pick StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase for HTTP keys, and name ConcurrentDictionary only when multiple threads write.

interviewTakeaways: List, Dictionary, HashSet, and Queue each answer one access pattern — append, key lookup, membership, FIFO.
Dictionary resizes by doubling buckets and rehashing; pre-size with expected count to avoid GC spikes.
Pass IEqualityComparer for string keys (Ordinal vs OrdinalIgnoreCase) and for custom struct keys.

60s: Append → List. Key lookup → Dictionary with capacity hint and comparer. Uniqueness → HashSet. FIFO → Queue. None are thread-safe or distributed — Channel for async pipes, Redis for cross-process.
Follow-up: what happens if GetHashCode changes after an item is inserted? (lookup breaks — keys must be immutable)
commonPitfalls: Saying Dictionary is always O(1) — ignores resize, collision chains, and bad hash distributions.
Strong answer: pre-size Dictionary, use HashSet for membership checks, pick IEqualityComparer explicitly for string and struct keys.
Using List.Contains in a hot loop instead of HashSet — O(n) per check versus O(1).
Sharing a List across SQS handler tasks without synchronization — corrupts the backing array.

jsTsCorrelations.concept: Map and Set versus object literals
jsTsCorrelations.note: JS Map uses reference equality for objects and SameValueZero for primitives. C# Dictionary uses IEqualityComparer — you must supply one for struct keys. JS {} coerces all keys to strings; Dictionary keeps Guid and int keys natively.
Record<string,T> is a typed object — keys are strings at run time. Dictionary<TKey,TValue> is a real hash table with configurable equality, closer to JS Map than to Record.
